newsitem.title: USA: PRESS DIGEST - Wall Street Journal - May 5.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Wall Street Journal - May 5.

text.p: The following stories were reported in Monday's electronic version of The Wall Street Journal:
* In April, U.S. unemployment fell to 4.9 percent of the workforce, the lowest level since 1973.
* According to Wall Street Journal calculation, corporate profits increased 18 percent in the first quarter compared to flat growth a year ago.
* Bre-X said an independent analysis showed its Busang property in Indonesia, touted as a massive gold deposit, was a fraud unprecedented in mining history.
* If federal regulators agree to cut fees paid local-phone companies for completing long-distance calls, AT&T has offered to lower its basic charges by up to 15 percent.
* The Dow Jones industrials closed up 94.72 points at 7,071.20 points, just shy of a record.
* According to people familiar with the matter, Compaq held high-level talks with Digital Equipment in 1995 and 1996 with an eye to a takeover of the firm but discussions broke down last summer.
* The Pacific Stock Exchange soon intends to start trading stocks listed on the New York Stock Exchange in sixteenths of a dollar.
* Goodyear Tire and the United Steelworkers, which represents its workers, reached a tentative accord to end a two-week strike at nine plants.
* Cordiant appointed New Zealand brewery executive Kevin Roberts as CEO of Saatchi & Saatchi Advertising.
* Three former Novell engineers were accused by the company of allegedly stealing software technology.
* Intel plans to unveil its Pentium II this week, seen as 20 percent to 50 percent faster than the Pentium line.
* A second representative is being brought in by public-health officials to the tobacco-settlement talks.
* Sony Corp's TriStar Pictures unit president Robert Cooper resigned after nine months on the job.

* Heard on the Street: A wonderful company. A beautiful company. A great company. With some media conglomerates under a cloud after the merger binge of recent years, money managers can't say enough in praise of Walt Disney and its chief Michael Eisner who keeps pushing out the profits from the Magic Kingdom.
* Credit markets: Enjoy the rally while it lasts, bond investors. Bonds turned in their best performance in almost a year last week but analysts sayd the market may not have much upside left in it.
